meta.title: Who really said "Leadership is the art of accomplishing more than the science of management says is possible"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Colin Powell really said it — but not in these words. His 2003 State Department lecture reads 'getting people to do more,' not 'accomplishing more.'
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Leadership is the art of accomplishing more than the science of management says is possible'?
meta.ogDescription: Powell called it 'my own personal definition' in 2003 — but said 'getting people to do more.' The popular wording traces to Oren Harari's books.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1937–2021 · Four-star general & 65th U.S. Secretary of State
answer.sourceLine: Powell genuinely owned this idea — but the famous wording is not the wording he used. In his 2003 Leadership Lecture at the State Department ↗ he said: “My own personal definition is that leadership is the art of getting people to do more than the science of management says is possible.” The circulating “accomplishing more” version is documented in Oren Harari’s books about Powell; Harari’s own source note traces it to Powell’s memoir My American Journey (1995), p. 258 — a page reference we have not been able to confirm. No Powell speech or transcript we found uses the “accomplishing more” wording.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: 2003 Leadership Lecture: Why Leadership Matters In The Department of State
Dean Acheson Auditorium, Washington, DC — 28 October 2003
The Leadership Secrets of Colin Powell (2002) and The Powell Principles (2003)

Oren Harari — the 2002 book closes its Prologue with the line and cites Powell’s memoir My American Journey (1995), p. 258, a page we have not been able to confirm; the 2003 book prints it as a front-matter epigraph with no citation at all

source.excerpt: Leaders make a difference. They don’t stand there. They do something. How do they make that difference? What is leadership all about? My own personal definition is that leadership is the art of getting people to do more than the science of management says is possible. … If the science of management says that the capacity of this organization is at 100 percent, good leaders take it to 110 percent.
trail: Oren Harari’s original compilation, “Quotations from Chairman Powell: A Leadership Primer” (©1996) ↗, gathers eighteen Powell lessons — and contains neither “science of management” nor “accomplishing more” anywhere in its text.

The two Harari books handle it differently, and the difference matters. In The Leadership Secrets of Colin Powell ↗ (2002) the sentence closes the Prologue — “Colin Powell has his own definition of leadership. As he puts it” — and the book’s back-of-book source notes cite it to Colin Powell with Joseph E. Persico, My American Journey (New York: Random House, 1995), p. 258. We have not been able to confirm that page. In The Powell Principles ↗ (2003) it is set alone on a front-matter page before the title page with no citation at all — verified against a scan of the printed front matter of the 2003 first printing.
Powell’s own formulation is on the record at the 2003 Leadership Lecture ↗, where he introduces it as “my own personal definition” and uses the phrase “getting people to do more.”

Wikiquote ↗ lists the popular wording under the heading “The Powell Principles (2003)” and describes that section as quotes of Powell from Harari’s book — not from anything Powell wrote or is transcribed as saying.
source.excerptNote: Powell’s own words, from the U.S. Department of State transcript. Note the verb: “getting people to do more,” not “accomplishing more.”

source.rightsNote: Two different sentences with two different rights answers. Powell’s own documented wording comes from a lecture delivered on 28 October 2003 and published as a U.S. Department of State transcript — a work of the U.S. Government, and so uncopyrightable under 17 U.S.C. §105. The circulating “accomplishing more” variant is another matter: its earliest verified printings are Oren Harari’s McGraw-Hill books of 2002 (© The McGraw-Hill Companies) and 2003 (© Oren Harari), both firmly in copyright. Harari’s 2002 notes cite the line to Powell’s My American Journey (Random House, 1995), p. 258, which would move it into a different rights bucket again — but we have not been able to confirm that page, so we treat the Harari titles as the controlling identifiable source and classify the variant conservatively as in copyright.
source.useLine: The wording in the credit above is Powell’s own, quoted from a U.S. Department of State transcript — a U.S. Government work (17 U.S.C. §105), free to reproduce. The circulating “accomplishing more” variant is different: it is identifiable only in Oren Harari’s in-copyright books (© 2002 The McGraw-Hill Companies; © 2003 Oren Harari), so if you use that version, keep it short, credit it, and get permission for commercial or published reuse.

author.name: Colin Powell
author.heading: Colin Powell
author.metaLine: 1937–2021 · U.S. Army four-star general, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff & 65th Secretary of State
author.bio: Powell served as the 12th Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff (1989–1993) and then as the 65th — and first Black American — U.S. Secretary of State (2001–2005). He described himself as having defended the flag, the Constitution and the country “for 35 years as a soldier,” and traced his own leadership education to “some sergeant grabbing you by the back of your neck” at Fort Benning when he was a brand-new second lieutenant. He talked about leadership constantly and largely extemporaneously — which is precisely why his best-known lines circulate in several slightly different wordings.

misattribution.heading: What actually went wrong
misattribution.intro: This one is unusual. The idea really is Powell’s, and he said so himself — but what circulates is a tidied-up version of his sentence, riding on a slide deck that most people believe he wrote.

items.who: “accomplishing more” replaces “getting people to do more”
items.why: Powell’s documented sentence puts people at the centre. In the very next breath at the 2003 Leadership Lecture ↗ he insisted, “The key word in that sentence, however, is ‘people.’” The popular rewrite deletes exactly that word.

items.who: Harari’s books — and his one citation points at a page we can’t check
items.why: The circulating wording is documented in Harari’s The Leadership Secrets of Colin Powell ↗ (2002), where it closes the Prologue and the book’s source notes credit it to My American Journey (New York: Random House, 1995), p. 258 — a page we have not been able to confirm, and Harari’s own 1996 compilation, drawn from the same memoir, contains no version of the sentence. In The Powell Principles ↗ (2003) it is printed on a front-matter page with no citation attached. So the honest position is narrower than “Powell never wrote it”: the only citation anyone offers is one we cannot verify.

items.who: credited to Powell as author; actually Harari’s 1996 compilation of Powell quotations — and the banner sentence is not among them
items.why: The much-forwarded “General Colin Powell – A Leadership Primer” PDF ↗ prints this sentence at the top of its title page, above eighteen numbered lessons. The lessons themselves really are Powell’s words — Harari says so in his ©1996 article ↗: “I present Powell’s words verbatim in bold—18 priceless lessons, to be exact.” What is Harari’s is the compilation, the commentary — and the banner sentence, which appears nowhere in that article.

misattribution.truthLine: Powell owned the idea outright — he called it “my own personal definition” at the State Department in 2003 ↗. Quote him by all means, but his words were “the art of getting people to do more than the science of management says is possible.”

context.heading: Why the missing word matters
lead: Powell was not theorising. He was talking to a room of State Department employees sitting on the floor and standing against the walls, and he had just dismissed the whole apparatus of leadership theory — “power up, power down, decentralize, centralize, theory X, theory Y” — as interesting but beside the point. His definition was meant as the plain-language alternative: if the science of management says an organisation’s capacity is 100 percent, a good leader takes it to 110, and a bad one takes it well below its designed capability.

The rewrite that travels the internet quietly deletes the one word Powell stopped to underline. Immediately after giving his definition he said the key word in that sentence is people — leadership is “not about organizations… not about plans… not about strategies.” “Accomplishing more” is smoother and more quotable, and it turns a claim about motivating human beings into a claim about output.
context.detailsSummary: How the tidier version took over
detailsBody: Powell had been drawing the same distinction for years. Government Executive reported in June 2001 that he told State Department workers, “Management is a science, leadership is an art, and I will be interested in identifying those people who are leaders, who really know how to turn people on.”

The compressed form appears in Oren Harari’s McGraw-Hill books. The 2002 Leadership Secrets closes its Prologue with it and, in the back-of-book notes, sources it to Powell’s My American Journey (1995), p. 258 — a page we have not been able to confirm; the 2003 Powell Principles simply prints it on a front-matter page before the title page with nothing attached. From there it was lifted onto the much-forwarded “A Leadership Primer” slide deck as a title-slide banner, and from the slide deck onto quote aggregators — each hop further from any transcript.
context.pull: The key word in that sentence, however, is ‘people.’

sourcesVerified.claim: Colin Powell said 'My own personal definition is that leadership is the art of getting people to do more than the science of management says is possible' at the 2003 Leadership Lecture, Dean Acheson Auditorium, Washington DC, 28 October 2003; he also said 'The key word in that sentence, however, is people' and gave the 100-percent-to-110-percent illustration.

The same 2003 lecture transcript, reproduced by GovLeaders.org, contains Powell's 'getting people to do more than the science of management says is possible' wording and does not contain 'accomplishing more'.

Oren Harari's ©1996 article 'Quotations from Chairman Powell: A Leadership Primer' contains no occurrence of 'science of management' or 'accomplishing more', and states of the eighteen lessons: 'With the exception of the occasional paraphrase to keep grammatical consistency (which will be noted), I present Powell's words verbatim in bold—18 priceless lessons, to be exact.'

Wikiquote lists 'Leadership is the art of accomplishing more than the science of management says is possible' in a section headed 'The Powell Principles (2003)', described as quotes of Powell from the book by Oren Harari; it is not placed in a Misattributed or Disputed section, and is not listed under My American Journey.

A scan of The Powell Principles (Oren Harari, McGraw-Hill, 2003) shows 'Leadership is the art of accomplishing more than the science of management says is possible.' printed alone on a front-matter epigraph page preceding the title page, with no citation; the same scan's copyright page reads 'Copyright © 2003 by Oren Harari' with McGraw-Hill as publisher. Working evidence only — not linked from the page, since it is an unauthorized full scan of an in-copyright title.

The circulated 'General Colin Powell – A Leadership Primer' PDF opens with the sentence 'Leadership is the art of accomplishing more than the science of management says is possible.' as a title-page epigraph above eighteen numbered lessons.

In Oren Harari's The Leadership Secrets of Colin Powell (McGraw-Hill, 2002) the sentence closes the Prologue — 'Colin Powell has his own definition of leadership. As he puts it: Leadership is the art of accomplishing more than the science of management says is possible.' — and the book's source notes, prefaced 'When the original provenance of a particular quote or story could be established, I have sourced it below', read: 'PROLOGUE "Leadership is the art of accomplishing more…" Colin Powell with Joseph E. Persico, My American Journey (New York: Random House, 1995), p. 258.' The copyright page reads 'Copyright © 2002 by The McGraw-Hill Companies'. Verified against a full-text scan used as working evidence only; the page cites the Internet Archive library record instead. We could NOT confirm p. 258 of My American Journey itself — every scan of the memoir is lending-restricted and no search corroborated the wording there.

Government Executive magazine, June 2001, quotes Powell telling State Department workers: 'Management is a science, leadership is an art, and I will be interested in identifying those people who are leaders, who really know how to turn people on.'
Colin Powell lived 1937–2021 and served as the 65th United States Secretary of State from 2001 to 2005, the first Black American to hold the office.
